name: Raloxifene (Evista)

lead: Raloxifene is a prescription SERM approved for osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction in postmenopausal women. Men use it off-label to shrink gynecomastia tissue and flatten the chest, including puberty-onset cases, often alongside or after tamoxifen.

It blocks estrogen action in breast tissue and mimics it in bone. Forum posters report shrinkage and some regrowth after stopping. Published evidence for this use is limited to small studies, such as a retrospective review in adolescent boys.

paras: It is a daily oral tablet taken for months. Users describe gradual shrinkage and often continue until results plateau.

The label carries a boxed warning for blood clots and stroke death; common effects include hot flashes, leg cramps and swelling. It is prescription-only, contraindicated in pregnancy, and not approved for men.

angle.text: Raloxifene is a SERM that men use off-label to shrink gynecomastia: it blocks estrogen action in breast tissue, which reduces gland tissue and flattens the chest. Forum posters report shrinkage and regrowth after stopping, and published evidence is limited to small studies.

lead: Raloxifene (brand name Evista) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) approved in the US for treating and preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and for reducing the risk of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or at high risk [1][2]. It acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast and uterine tissue [2][3].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it is discussed as an off-label oral option for gynecomastia, including puberty-onset gynecomastia, often alongside or after tamoxifen [4][5]. Published evidence for that use consists of small studies, for example a retrospective review in adolescent boys; it is not an approved indication [1][3].

paras: Raloxifene is used for postmenopausal osteoporosis, though it is less preferred than bisphosphonates, and for reducing breast cancer risk in high-risk postmenopausal women [1]. It is not indicated for treating invasive breast cancer or reducing recurrence [2]. It does not relieve hot flashes and may worsen them [3]. An early trial examined its effects on bone mineral density, cholesterol and the uterine lining in postmenopausal women [6].

A small retrospective chart review reported that raloxifene was effective for pubertal gynecomastia in adolescent boys; Wikipedia notes other SERMs also treat gynecomastia [1]. Grokipedia, citing that kind of data, describes a greater than 50 percent reduction in breast tissue volume in most of the treated boys, but this is a small off-label dataset [3]. Looksmax.org posters describe using raloxifene after or alongside tamoxifen for gynecomastia and ask whether it returns after stopping; other posters argue surgery is preferable [4][5].

Common effects are hot flashes, leg cramps, peripheral edema, flu syndrome, joint pain and sweating [2]. The label carries a boxed warning for increased risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and for increased risk of death from stroke in women with coronary heart disease or elevated risk; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in people with a history of venous thromboembolism [2]. Unlike tamoxifen it does not increase uterine hyperplasia or endometrial cancer risk [1].

Raloxifene binds estrogen receptors and its agonist or antagonist action depends on recruitment of coactivators and corepressors to target gene promoters in each tissue [2]. Structural work in 1997 described the molecular basis of agonism and antagonism at the estrogen receptor [7]. Oral bioavailability is about 2 percent owing to first-pass metabolism; it is metabolised by glucuronidation and has a half-life of roughly 28 to 33 hours [1].

In the MORE trial of 7,705 postmenopausal women, raloxifene reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures [8] and reduced breast cancer incidence [9]. The STAR trial compared raloxifene with tamoxifen in high-risk postmenopausal women and found similar invasive-breast-cancer prevention with a lower thromboembolism risk [1][10]. Smaller registered trials have tested raloxifene in schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease and endometriosis [11]. No controlled trial in men with gynecomastia was identified; the evidence is the small retrospective review described above [1].
